category.name: Threat Intelligence
category.description: Malware, phishing, scanning and indicator-of-compromise data. Built for SOC and CERT work, but equally useful to journalists and researchers: these are the sources that connect a suspicious domain to a known campaign, and they are mostly free.

tools.name: VirusTotal
tools.summary: Analyses files and URLs against many antivirus engines and aggregates community and infrastructure context.
tools.description:
VirusTotal, owned by Google, scans submitted files and URLs with a large panel of antivirus engines and sandboxes, and stores the results alongside a wealth of derived context: which domains a file contacted, which files were downloaded from a domain, which URLs resolve to an IP, and community comments and votes.

The relationship data is what makes it an investigative tool rather than a scanner. Given one malicious domain you can find the files that communicated with it, then the other domains those files contacted, and map a campaign's infrastructure without ever executing anything yourself.

The hazard is severe and repeatedly realised. Uploaded files are shared with the security industry and, at many access levels, retrievable by other users. Organisations have leaked confidential documents, internal tooling and even credentials by uploading a file to check it. Never upload a document you did not author and do not own, never upload anything containing confidential or source-identifying material, and prefer searching by hash — which discloses nothing — over uploading. If you have the file, compute its hash locally and search that first.
tools.costNotes: A free public API is available with a registered account, rate-limited to a small number of requests per minute with daily and monthly quotas that reset on a published schedule. Uploading a new file does not itself consume API quota, but retrieving the resulting report does. Premium API tiers add higher rates, retrospective search and additional data.
tools.legalNotes: Files you upload are shared with security vendors and partners and may be retrievable by other users of the service. This is by design and is stated in the terms, and it has caused real, documented confidential-data exposure. Do not upload material belonging to a third party, material from a source, or anything under legal privilege or embargo. Searching an existing hash, URL or domain discloses only that indicator and is much safer.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Engine verdicts are the single most misread output in security research: a small number of detections on an otherwise clean file is very often a false positive, and a clean result is common for targeted malware that no vendor has seen. Never report a detection count as a determination. The relationship and infrastructure data is more dependable and is where the investigative value actually lies.
tools.confidenceNotes: Free public API rate limits, quota reset behaviour and the upload-versus-report quota distinction were confirmed against VirusTotal's own documentation during this review. Premium pricing was not verified.

tools.name: URLhaus
tools.summary: Free community database of URLs distributing malware, with fully open bulk feeds.
tools.description:
URLhaus, operated by abuse.ch, collects and publishes URLs observed distributing malware. Each entry records the URL, the hosting infrastructure, the malware family where identified, the reporter and the current status of the URL.

It is free without restriction, including bulk downloads and an API, which is unusual in this space and makes it directly usable for research at scale. For investigators the useful operations are searching a domain or IP to see whether it has ever been reported as hosting malware, and using the dataset to identify hosting providers and networks that appear repeatedly — a good indicator of bulletproof hosting.

Limits: it holds what the community reported, so coverage is a sample rather than a census, and absence means nothing. Entries record what was observed at a point in time, and a URL long since cleaned will still appear with its historical report.
tools.costNotes: Free including full bulk feeds and API access. An account improves API usage but the core data is openly published. Operated by abuse.ch, hosted within an academic institution.
tools.legalNotes: Openly published for defensive and research use, with permissive terms. The dataset lists URLs to live malicious content — treat every listed URL as hostile and never fetch one from a machine or network you care about. Reporting that a domain hosted malware is a factual claim about its operator and should be dated and attributed to the specific URLhaus entry.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Community-reported and generally accurate, with a status field showing whether a URL is still live. Coverage is partial by nature. Malware family attribution comes from automated classification and reporter labelling and is not authoritative — treat family names as indicative. Historical entries persist after cleanup, so always read the dates before characterising a host's current state.
tools.confidenceNotes: Long-established and widely relied-upon community service. Not fetched during this review.

tools.name: MalwareBazaar
tools.summary: Free repository of malware samples and their metadata, searchable by hash, family, tag and signature.
tools.description:
MalwareBazaar, also from abuse.ch, collects malware samples shared by the community and publishes their metadata: hashes, file type, first-seen date, identified family, YARA rule matches, and the tags and signatures associated with them.

Its investigative use rarely involves downloading anything. Searching a hash tells you whether a file has been seen before, when it first appeared, and what family it belongs to — which places a sample in a campaign timeline. Searching by family or tag shows the spread of a campaign over time. This is metadata research, and it is the safe way to use the service.

Samples themselves are downloadable, and unless you are a malware analyst with an isolated environment and a reason, you should not. Downloading live malware onto a working machine is how investigations turn into incidents.
tools.costNotes: Free, including API and bulk access. Sample downloads are available under the service's conditions. Operated by abuse.ch.
tools.legalNotes: Possession and distribution of malware samples is regulated in some jurisdictions, and a legitimate research purpose is not a universal defence — check your own position before downloading anything. Some jurisdictions treat possession of tools capable of causing unauthorised modification as an offence subject to intent. Metadata search carries none of this exposure and is almost always sufficient for OSINT purposes.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Metadata is accurate and well structured, and first-seen dates are useful for campaign timelines. Family attribution is derived from automated classification and community tagging, and different sources name the same family differently — do not treat a label as authoritative. Coverage is a community sample, not a complete corpus.
tools.confidenceNotes: Long-established community service from a well-known operator. Not fetched during this review.

tools.name: ThreatFox
tools.summary: Free community feed of indicators of compromise linked to malware families and campaigns.
tools.description:
ThreatFox is abuse.ch's indicator-of-compromise database: IP addresses, domains, URLs and hashes reported as associated with specific malware families and campaigns, each with a confidence level, a reporter and a first-seen date.

Its value in an investigation is fast attribution context. Given a suspicious domain you can check whether anyone has reported it as command-and-control infrastructure for a named family, which immediately reframes what you are looking at. The confidence field is unusually useful because it is explicit — most feeds leave you guessing how sure the reporter was.

Everything is free including bulk export and API, so it integrates into automated enrichment without a commercial agreement.

Limits: crowd-sourced attribution is exactly as reliable as the reporter, and malware family names are inconsistently applied across the industry. An IOC listed under a family name is a lead about that family, not a confirmation.
tools.costNotes: Free, including full API and bulk export. An account enables submission and higher API usage.
tools.legalNotes: Open data intended for defensive and research use. Listing an indicator is an assertion by a community reporter, not an adjudicated finding — publishing that a company's server is malware infrastructure on the strength of an IOC listing alone is a defamation risk, particularly where the server was compromised rather than complicit.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Useful and current, with explicit confidence levels that should be read and reported. Attribution quality varies by reporter, family naming is inconsistent across the industry, and indicators go stale quickly — infrastructure is reused, and today's malicious IP is next month's legitimate shared host. Always check the first-seen date and consider what has changed since.
tools.confidenceNotes: Established community service from a well-known operator. Not fetched during this review.

tools.name: LevelBlue Open Threat Exchange (OTX)
tools.summary: Free community threat-intelligence platform where researchers publish indicator sets as 'pulses'.
tools.description:
Open Threat Exchange is a community platform on which researchers publish 'pulses' — curated sets of indicators tied to a campaign, a malware family or an incident, usually with narrative context and references. It originated with AlienVault, passed through AT&T Cybersecurity, and now operates under LevelBlue branding following that business's separation, while retaining the alienvault.com domain.

What makes it useful beyond a raw feed is the narrative. A pulse typically explains what the indicators are, who reported them and why they are believed related, sometimes with links to published research. That context is what turns an IP address into a lead you can act on. Searching an indicator shows every pulse referencing it, which quickly reveals whether infrastructure you are looking at is already documented.

Limits: contribution quality varies enormously. Some pulses are rigorous professional research; others are automated dumps or copies of other pulses with no added verification, which creates an illusion of independent corroboration when several pulses actually derive from one source. Check who published a pulse and whether its references are real before treating it as confirmation.
tools.costNotes: Free with a registered account, including API access for retrieving and subscribing to pulses. Positioned as a community offering alongside the operator's commercial products.
tools.legalNotes: Open community platform; contributed content is published by its authors and its accuracy is not warranted by the operator. Republishing an attribution claim found in a pulse without checking its basis carries the usual defamation exposure. Note that your subscriptions and searches are visible to the operator.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Wide coverage and genuinely useful context, but variable contributor quality is the defining limitation. Pulses copying other pulses produce apparent corroboration that does not exist — trace a claim to its original source before counting it as independent. Indicators age quickly and many pulses are never updated.
tools.confidenceNotes: Confirmed during this review as live and operating under LevelBlue branding at the alienvault.com domain, with the community platform and API intact.

tools.name: GreyNoise
tools.summary: Identifies which IPs are mass-scanning the internet, so you can tell background noise from a targeted event.
tools.description:
GreyNoise operates a global sensor network and classifies the IP addresses it sees conducting internet-wide scanning: what they scan for, whether they are benign research scanners, known-malicious actors, or common business services.

The question it answers is one no other tool answers well: is this IP interesting? An IP that scanned your infrastructure and also scanned the entire internet that day is background noise. An IP that touched only you is a targeted event. That distinction removes an enormous amount of wasted analytical effort and is regularly the difference between an incident and a non-event.

For investigation more broadly, it also gives context on an IP found in logs or in another dataset — a mass scanner appearing in a victim's logs usually means nothing at all.

Limits: it only knows about IPs that touched its sensors, so a targeted actor who never scans broadly is invisible to it, which is precisely the actor you most care about. Absence from GreyNoise is not a clean bill of health.
tools.costNotes: A free Community API and the public Visualizer allow IP lookups; free-tier accounts have been limited to roughly 50 searches per week, counted across both the Community API and the Visualizer together. Paid platform tiers add higher limits, historical data and additional modules.
tools.legalNotes: Passive lookup against GreyNoise's own observations; nothing is sent to the IP you query and the operator of that address is not notified. Standard commercial terms apply to bulk use and redistribution.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Well-regarded classification with clear methodology, and unusually good at what it claims to do. The boundary of that claim is the key limitation: it characterises mass-scanning behaviour, not targeted activity, so a null result carries no defensive assurance. Classifications reflect observed behaviour over a window and an IP's character can change when it is reassigned.
tools.confidenceNotes: Free Community API and Visualizer availability confirmed during this review, including the shared free-tier allowance of approximately 50 searches per week across both. Paid tier pricing was not verified.

tools.name: AbuseIPDB
tools.summary: Community database of IP addresses reported for abusive activity, with category and confidence scoring.
tools.description:
AbuseIPDB collects reports of abusive network behaviour — brute forcing, scanning, spam, web attacks — against IP addresses, and computes an abuse confidence score from the volume, recency and diversity of reports.

For quick triage of an IP found in logs or in another dataset it is fast and free, and the report categories give a sense of what the address has been doing. The reporter diversity matters more than the raw count: many reports from one source is much weaker than a few from unrelated ones.

Limits worth taking seriously. Reports are unverified and unadjudicated. Shared hosting, NAT gateways, VPN exit nodes and carrier-grade NAT addresses accumulate reports generated by a small number of bad actors among many innocent users, and the address itself is not meaningfully culpable. Reassignment means historical reports may concern an entirely different customer. The score is a crowd signal, not a finding, and treating it as one produces both unjust blocking and wrong conclusions.
tools.costNotes: Free tier with a registered account provides a daily allowance of API checks and reports; higher-volume and commercial use requires a paid plan or a webmaster verification for your own address space. Current allowances were not verified in this review.
tools.legalNotes: Community-reported allegations, not findings. Publishing that an IP or its assigned organisation engaged in attacks on the basis of AbuseIPDB reports alone is an unverified allegation with defamation risk, particularly where the address belongs to a hosting provider or a compromised third party. Reports may include personal data where an address is residential.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Useful as a very rough triage signal and nothing more. Reports are unverified, easily skewed by a handful of noisy reporters, and systematically unfair to shared and dynamic addresses. IP reassignment makes older reports misleading. Rated 2 because the confidence score invites exactly the over-reliance the data cannot support. Always corroborate with GreyNoise or your own observations before acting.
tools.confidenceNotes: Long-established community service. Not fetched during this review; free-tier allowances were not verified.

tools.name: MISP
tools.summary: Open-source threat intelligence platform for storing, correlating and sharing structured indicators.
tools.description:
MISP is the de facto open standard for structured threat-intelligence sharing between organisations, CERTs and ISACs. You run your own instance, record events and attributes, and it automatically correlates across everything you hold — surfacing that an indicator in today's incident also appeared in something you recorded eighteen months ago.

For investigative teams its relevance is less about threat sharing than about structured case data under your own control. It provides a rigorous model for recording indicators with provenance, confidence and relationships, and it is self-hosted, so sensitive material never leaves your infrastructure. The taxonomy and tagging system supports traffic-light-protocol handling constraints, which matters when material comes with sharing restrictions attached.

Limits: it is genuinely heavyweight. Running and maintaining an instance is a real commitment, the data model takes time to learn, and it is substantial overkill for an investigator working alone on a handful of cases.
tools.costNotes: Free and open source under an AGPL licence. Costs are hosting and operational effort. Commercial support and hosted instances are available from third parties.
tools.legalNotes: Self-hosting keeps you in full control of the data and in full possession of the obligations that come with it: an instance holding indicators that identify individuals is a personal-data system needing lawful basis, access control, retention and deletion. Sharing communities operate under distribution and traffic-light-protocol rules that are contractual as well as conventional — honour them. The AGPL has real obligations if you modify and offer the software over a network.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Mature, widely deployed and actively maintained, with a well-specified data model. Reliability of the content is entirely a function of what you and your sharing partners put in — MISP correlates faithfully, including correlating noise into a compelling-looking graph. Discipline about attribute confidence and source at entry time is what makes it useful rather than misleading.
tools.confidenceNotes: Long-established, widely deployed open-source project with institutional backing. Not fetched during this review.

tools.name: CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog
tools.summary: Authoritative US government list of vulnerabilities with confirmed active exploitation in the wild.
tools.description:
The Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue is CISA's list of CVEs for which there is reliable evidence of active exploitation. It is short by design — a small fraction of published CVEs — and each entry carries the affected product, a required remediation date for US federal agencies, and the date it was added.

The signal is what makes it valuable. Vulnerability databases list everything; KEV lists what is actually being exploited, which is a completely different and far more actionable question. For an investigator examining a compromise, checking whether an exposed service on the victim's infrastructure has a KEV-listed vulnerability quickly generates a credible hypothesis about initial access.

It is free, published as machine-readable data, and requires no account.

Limits: it reflects exploitation that has been observed and confirmed, so it lags the beginning of exploitation, and absence from KEV does not mean a vulnerability is not being used. It is US-authored and skews toward products relevant to US federal agencies.
tools.costNotes: Free, no account, published as downloadable JSON and CSV as well as a web catalogue.
tools.legalNotes: US government public data, freely usable. Carries a binding remediation obligation for US federal civilian agencies and is widely adopted as a de facto standard elsewhere; it is not a legal obligation for private organisations outside that scope, and describing it as one is a common error.
tools.reliabilityNotes: Authoritative and conservatively curated — an entry means the agency assessed the evidence of exploitation as reliable, which is a high bar. That conservatism is also the limitation: the list lags real-world exploitation and is deliberately incomplete. Never read absence as an indication that a vulnerability is not being exploited.
tools.confidenceNotes: Established and actively maintained US government catalogue. Not fetched during this review; CISA has reorganised URLs before, so confirm the current entry point.
